utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. Case Number IT-99-36-T, The Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can follow in a language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please, sit down. Appearances, Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. On day 284, the last day of evidence, it's Joanna Korner, Julian Nicholls, Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Korner, and good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman with David Cunningham, Aleksandar Vujic, and Cynthia Dresden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And good morning to you and your team. Before we bring in the witness, the meeting that was scheduled for -- or that is still scheduled for 11.30 this morning may run a hitch. The problem is Mr. Roberts is at least until now indisposed, and he is the one with whom I have been dealing and who knows most of the details, some of which I asked him to keep for himself. So he has instructed one of the other members of the staff to stand for him, to take it over, but I'm not that happy to proceed with the meeting in the absence of Mr. Roberts. Now, Mr. Roberts also told me that he will do his level best to try and come over at 11.30 for the meeting. So after all, we might well be able to proceed. So I will keep you posted later on. I will keep you updated. Although we can still meet in his absence and discuss certain matters, but certainly not be able to cover the whole territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it would probably make more sense just to have the one meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I think. This has just come up now, a few minutes before the start of this hearing. I have been actually trying to get hold of the other legal officer, but he was apparently busy in some other room and I didn't know exactly which room, so I didn't have the time, the physical time, to track him down and see what the position is. But I will keep you posted. I suppose by 10.30 I should more or less know if Mr. Roberts is coming over. If he is, then obviously I will contact you and the meeting will take place as scheduled. If not, we'll have it postponed. But Mr. Roberts has got serious back trouble this morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I have every sympathy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know what it means, too. So it's not likely that we will have the meeting this morning anyway. Thanks. Yes, shall we admit the witness. Is it in closed session?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We had requested closed session, Your Honour. I don't think we got a written response from the Defence, and I think that the Court had decided it would question the witness, and then come to a decision. But I can confirm that she requests closed session, and I think the reasons are valid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to go into private session for just a moment for a preliminary matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour was about to deal with the meeting. That will be in your Chambers, will it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, because I had asked for the meeting to be held in Room 177. However, we were late for that. It had been taken by someone else. And rather than going through the whole exercise of finding another room somewhere else, I decided on my Chambers. So 11.00, when we finish in my Chambers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, say about 10 minutes, I need to collect the papers that relate to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. I mean, I think we will need to arrange for you, Mr. Ackerman, but someone from my team will look after that. I wish to make a statement, and this is a statement on -- not only on my own behalf, but also on behalf of Judge Janu and Judge Taya, statement on behalf of the Trial Chamber. Yesterday, Mr. Ackerman on behalf of Mr. Brdjanin stated that the Defence rested its case. It was already past quarter to 2.00. I knew that today we would also have the last witness testifying, so I did not make any statement yesterday. I'm going to make a statement today. So yesterday, the Defence rested its case. Today, we can say that we have concluded the rebuttal and rejoinder case, although there has not been a rejoinder. In other words, we can safely state that the evidence -- evidentiary stage of this trial has finally come to an end. It took us 284 days of hearings, 284 sittings, to reach this stage. But this is not a minor case by any means. This is undoubtedly the biggest and most complicated case outside -- apart from -- after the Milosevic case. During these two years, the Trial Chamber, we did our best, we endeavoured to do our best to give each one of you as much room as possible with the least restrictions possible, that is, to make your case respectively. And this we tried to do and achieve with full respect to the Rules of a fair trial according to the best standards of this Tribunal. Also, without taxing unduly its resources. As in every case, we have had, of course, our ups and downs, our difficult moments. But overall, I can state on behalf of the Trial Chamber that it is thanks -- ultimately thanks to both of you that we have managed to bring this stage of the proceedings to a close, more or less according to the schedule which we had set way back. I said thanks to you, because you have shown professionalism throughout these two years, great professionalism in your work. You have done your best not to waste the time of this Trial Chamber. And in a great majority of cases, you responded positively when we appealled for your understanding and cooperation. So I thank you, Ms. Korner, and you, Mr. Ackerman, for your excellent work and for your very positive contribution in this trial. Our appreciation and our thanks, gratitude, also -- is also extended, of course, to the other members of your respective teams. I do wish, however, to signal one person in particular, it's you, Mr. Cunningham. I also wish to thank you. Your entry on stage in these proceedings has certainly made a change and enabled Mr. Ackerman to proceed smoothly with the case at a moment of crisis, first because of his ill health, but also because of the more or less contemporaneous termination of Mr. Trbojevic's assignment of co-counsel by the Registrar. We now have a few more months to go before we can bring this case to an end. These months will, of course, be crucial and will involve us and our staff in detailed deliberations. Of course, we will be looking forward to your final pleadings and submissions, which we have reason to believe will be of the same high standard as those of your previous submissions in this case. Once more, Judge Janu, Judge Taya, and myself wish to thank you for your cooperation and your good work. We also wish to thank all those staff members who have worked with us in this case, and I am referring to the members of the Registrar's office, to the members of the victims and witnesses section, the interpreters, who have a very difficult job, and the technical staff who have together many a time made it possible for the Trial Chamber to sit beyond the normal hours to the benefit of the case and to the overall benefit of the Tribunal in general. I think this ought to be acknowledged publicly, and I am trying to do that today. Of course, last but not least, I should like to thank the very hard-working members of our legal staff who have been with us working Saturdays, working Sundays sometimes, like you, Ms. Korner, and you, Mr. Ackerman, and the respective members of your team have been doing. I also wish to thank the members of the security section of this Tribunal who have secured the order in which these proceedings have been conducted. With that, I think we can rise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know, Your Honours, say -- I have to ask Your Honours to come back for one moment to reality which is: Your Honours have got to give us a ruling on the -- before you rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, the -- our decision on all those documents is as follows: We had some difficulty only with regard to General Talic's statement, but we have, after having gone through case law, come to the conclusion that we should not exclude it a priori, and that together with the other documents that have been objected to, they -- it will remain in the records. In other words, they are being admitted. We wish to make a point clear, however, particularly with regard to this document which is essentially a statement made by a co-accused at a time when technically speaking he was still accused before this Tribunal in a way which now results in the impossibility of the Prosecution being able to cross-examine the witness on the most fundamental parts contained in that statement. This is of fundamental importance. We have taken this into consideration, and it will, of course, affect our decision later on as to whether to give this document, together with some other, any weight, any weight at all. But our decision at the moment is that we cannot exclude it a priori on the basis of unreliability or on the basis of any of the points which have been made in some of the case law that we consulted. So all the documents that we discussed yesterday, if needs to be, I will repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let me find the list. And we are talking of DB288 and 289, DB344, DB345, which is precisely the statement that was taken from General Momir Talic in December of 1992, that is, subsequent to his release, provisional release, and finally DB361 to 373, being the NIWD -- extracts from the NIWD reports. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I have to make it clear to Your Honour -- to Your Honours that in normal circumstances we would appeal the admission, in particular, of General Talic statement. It's not sworn. It complies with none of the Rules at all. I take the view, and the reason I'm saying this is if the OTP doesn't appeal that's a sign that we accept the ruling, I take the view that there's no likelihood of receiving a decision from the Appeals Chamber before we have to put in the final brief, and therefore it's to clog up the Appeals Chamber even longer. But I need to make that absolutely clear on the record so that in future if this comes up again it can't be taken that the OTP accepted this ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I fully understand that, Ms. Korner. And we want to make it clear that we are fully aware of the shortcomings of this statement, that it is not a sworn statement, that there is no possibility of cross-examination, that it was not taken in any manner, one of the manners that the Rules indicate, et cetera. But all these considerations do not necessarily lead to the conclusion of inadmissibility from the very word go. It's still a question of reliability at the end of the day, and we are basing ourselves more or less on the line that case law, few judgements that we have, have taken on this matter referring particularly to how our Rules are conceived. In your jurisdiction or in my jurisdiction, this would not have been admitted for sure, this statement. In our case, we have this general rule which does not necessarily override other Rules, but which needs to be read in conjunction with other Rules that we have. And our decision is to prefer to reserve our decision on what weight, if at all, to give to this final -- to this document, to our final deliberations. And this applies not just to this document, it applies to several other documents that we have in this case. And I can tell you straight away that I personally attach a lot of importance to the fact that there may be cases where we have statements made by persons who have not been brought here or who cannot be brought here to be cross-examined or to answer questions in relation to the contents of those documents. This is something which I need hardly emphasise. It's basic. And I think it also applies to General Talic's statement that was obtained by...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've made the position clear. While I'm on the topic of the Appeals Chamber, Your Honour I was assured that we would have a ruling by the first or second week of February. We are now in the third week of February. We have had no ruling on the appeal in respect of the joint criminal enterprise 3 decision by Your Honours. I don't know whether Your Honours have any power to urge the Appeals Chamber to give us a decision, please, within the next week. But it really is important because we're all writing our final briefs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We certainly do not have power. But we will try and do our best. I know that the President at the moment has got enough on his mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we will do our best because it's also in our best interests to know --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think for all parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- where we stand in that. Today I had in mind of dealing -- to deal with our programme for the next month.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just mention there's still outstanding Mr. Ackerman's application in respect of the witness who didn't attend for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know whether Your Honours had a chance to look at the decision --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- which in fact, of course, it was Judge Wald presiding. And it goes a lot -- I did manage to recover the article. Your Honour, we've also got the case referred to in the decision which is Fulantelli [phoen] and St. Angelo against Italy, the court of -- European Court of Human Rights. Your Honour, we would submit that although this witness wasn't cross-examined and of course Your Honours have to take that into account, I made an error yesterday. I thought cross-examination had started, but it hadn't. But nonetheless, under the decision that was made by the European Court of Human Rights, this is not fatal to the evidence remaining part of the record. The right of the accused to examine the witnesses against him must occasionally yield in appropriate circumstances in the interests of considering the maximum amount of relevant evidence. This evidence wasn't the sole evidence of -- in relation to the events that were described unto the particular person. It was to that extent cumulative. Your Honour, I can give the, Your Honour, names of the pseudonyms of the other witness who is testified to the same type of events involving the particular person. And it is not direct evidence against the accused personally. So in those circumstances, I would invite Your Honours to allow this evidence to remain with, of course, the major caveat that no cross-examination was able to take place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Obviously. That is again crucial. Yes, Mr. Ackerman. Do you have anything to state on this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, only this: We do operate a little differently from most of the courts that would be members of the European Community. We do have specific rules about those instances when witnesses do not have to be brought here for cross-examination. And this witness was brought here for direct and cross-examination for I would say good and valid reason. And for reasons beyond everyone's control, the situation developed that he was not able to be cross-examined. And so it's -- in my view, it should be treated as if he had never come in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I come from a jurisdiction where that wouldn't be the case, Mr. Ackerman, because more or less we apply the system -- even if I were presiding over a trial, a normal trial with a panel of jurors, and we have a statement -- an occurrence identical to this, the consequence, legal consequence, is not to throw out the statement or the evidence simply because there is no longer the possibility of the Defence to cross-examine that witness. But to put all this to the jurors and explain to the jurors the importance that they need to attach to the fact that that witness has not been cross-examined and that this should carry its weight. Of course, if I am proceeding without a jury, then obviously the matter assumes even -- this legal consideration assumes even more weight. So our decision basically is to have the testimony of this person remain in the records, and of course I am making it abundantly clear, I hope, that we will, as we come to examine what weight to give to this testimony, if at all, give all due consideration to the fact that you have been unable to cross-examine this witness, Mr. Ackerman, due to no fault of your own or of your client. So that's the position.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I finally, going back to the very kind remarks that Your Honours made, just mention this. Your Honours have seen of course counsel appearing in front of you. Behind the scenes, as I also imagine is the case with the Defence, there have been a number of people, and in particular language staff who have had to work weekends as well and really have worked beyond the call of duty to assist the Prosecution team in making sure that the case went as smoothly as it could. And I think it's only right that they should be mentioned as well as the investigators who Your Honours have seen have done an enormous amount to help to put this case together. And finally, I feel I should mention specifically Ms. Gustin and the case manager unit generally. The counsel can do a good job once they're in court provided they know how to do a good job. But we couldn't actually operate without the exhibits, the papers, and everything being got together by the case manager unit. And so I think it's only right they should be acknowledged in open court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Korner. I associate myself. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I can't be left out of this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No one would dare do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me start with all of the staff that serves this Court who have just done a remarkable, stellar job as we have gone through these two years, and I want to my own express personal gratitude to all of them, the translators, the court reporters, the court staff, the Registry staff, all of these people. We have had serving us a number of interns that you are aware of. I don't know if you're aware that these people all worked without any remuneration or compensation at all. And they all did a great deal of work and contributed a great deal to our ability to keep this case on track and get to where we got today. I must second, third, and fourth your remarks regarding Mr. Cunningham. I'm astounded at how quickly he was able to get up to speed in this case. He read an enormous amount of material in going through all the transcripts and documents in this case and spent enormous number of hours for which there's no hope of him being compensated by the Registry. He didn't work within the very severe limitations the Registry put upon him, but served this Court in the highest tradition of our profession. And finally, I must say this: I am frequently asked what kind of a judge I appreciate, and my standard answer is I like judges who know, believe in, and apply the law, and who otherwise leave lawyers alone to try the case. And I can say that this Trial Chamber has met that in spades, and I really do appreciate being allowed to try my case. And I'm sure Ms. Korner feels the same way. We were allowed to be the kind of lawyers we would like to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if there were times when we were hard, and yes, Judge Janu tells me that there were such times, but she is excluding herself. We want you to understand that the intention was not -- nothing but to try and get this case -- move ahead, try to bring it within a time frame which in one way would be acceptable; the second -- at the same time, it would ensure, maintain the rights which each one of you had to present your respective case properly. We may have been sometimes difficult. I understand. It's not the first time in my life that I have been difficult. Most of the time, I have had understanding, and I'm sure that I have your understanding as well. Thank you once more. My legal officer, Mr. Roberts, will eventually contact you both to short of revise the schedule that we have for final pleadings and the rest. And if there are requests on your part that you would like to make, we will be prepared to entertain them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, all I think we're concerned about is that Your Honour's not thinking of bringing forward the date of the 26th of March for filing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, we are not -- we do not intend to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Because we have been working towards that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we are happy with the way things turned out to be, that we are finishing the evidentiary stage before the end of February. So it's not our intention to touch anything from the schedule that we more or less had suggested to you. Rather, we are telling you if you need more time, if you have problems, please come back to us and we will see where -- how we can address those to your mutual satisfaction. Okay? Or to our mutual satisfaction. What time shall we meet in my Chambers?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would Your Honour say midday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I assume someone will come get me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 11.47 a.m.
